summary: Idebenone is a synthetic short-chain analog of coenzyme Q10 that acts as an antioxidant and mitochondrial electron carrier. It is NOT FDA-approved; in the European Union it is authorized as Raxone for the treatment of visual impairment in adolescents and adults with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON). It donates electrons directly to complex III, bypassing a defective complex I, helping restore cellular ATP production and reduce oxidative stress in retinal ganglion cells. It is generally well tolerated; reddish discoloration of urine is common and benign.
indications: Treatment of visual impairment in adolescent and adult patients with Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) - EMA-authorized (Raxone)
Historically studied (without robust approval) in Friedreich ataxia and as a cognitive/antioxidant agent - not established indications

moa: Idebenone is a short-chain benzoquinone structurally related to coenzyme Q10. In its reduced form it can transfer electrons directly to mitochondrial respiratory chain complex III, bypassing a dysfunctional complex I. This restores mitochondrial ATP synthesis in cells with impaired complex I (as in LHON) and supports survival and function of retinal ganglion cells. Its quinone moiety also acts as an antioxidant, scavenging reactive oxygen species and protecting cell membranes and mitochondria from lipid peroxidation.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to idebenone or any excipient
relative: Severe hepatic or renal impairment (limited data)
monitor: Visual acuity and optical coherence tomography in LHON
Recognition of benign chromaturia versus hematuria

preg: There are limited or no adequate data on the use of idebenone in pregnant women. As a precaution, it is preferable to avoid use during pregnancy unless the potential benefit clearly outweighs the risk (per EMA SmPC).
lact: It is unknown whether idebenone or its metabolites are excreted in human milk, and a risk to the breastfed infant cannot be excluded; a decision should be made to stop breastfeeding or to avoid the drug.
renal: No specific dosage recommendation is available for renal impairment because data are limited; use with caution and clinical monitoring.
hepatic: Idebenone is metabolized in the liver (glucuronidation and sulfation); there is limited information in hepatic impairment, so use with caution and monitor for accumulation or hepatic effects.

pearls: Not FDA-approved; in the EU it is authorized as Raxone for Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (source: EMA SmPC/BNF rather than FDA label)
Acts as a CoQ10 analog that bypasses complex I by feeding electrons to complex III
Reddish-brown urine is an expected, benign effect - reassure patients to avoid confusion with hematuria
Best visual responses in LHON tend to occur when treatment is started early after vision loss
Take with food to improve its otherwise variable absorption
missed: Take the missed dose with food as soon as you remember on the same day; if it is almost time for the next dose, skip it and resume the usual three-times-daily schedule. Do not double up.
overdose: There is limited experience with idebenone overdose; doses well above the therapeutic range have been used in studies with a favorable tolerability profile. Management is supportive and symptomatic with monitoring; there is no specific antidote.
